title: The Niphal

objectives.can: Recognise and parse Niphal forms and say how the verb's Niphal is related to its Qal.

explanation.summary: The Niphal is the second commonest stem after the Qal. It is marked by a nun at the front of the word in the qatal and the participle, and by a doubled first root consonant in the yiqtol, the imperative and the infinitives. Its relation to the Qal differs from verb to verb: it is often passive or reflexive, but not always.

sections.heading: The nun in the qatal and the participle
body: In the qatal and the participle, the Niphal puts a nun before the first root consonant, with an i-vowel: נִשְׁמַר, נִלְחַם. The rest of the qatal follows the Qal pattern of endings. נִשְׁבַּעְתִּי in Genesis 22:16 is a qatal, first singular, with the same ending -תִּי that you know from the Qal.

The participle has the same prefix but a long vowel in the last syllable: נִלְחָם is a participle, נִלְחַם a qatal. The difference is easily lost in pause, at the end of a clause, where a qatal can also have the long vowel. The edition analyses נִלְחָם in 1 Kings 22:46 as a qatal. Context decides when the vowels do not.

sections.heading: The nun disappears: yiqtol, imperative, infinitives
body: In the other forms the nun does not appear at the front. In the yiqtol it has joined the first root consonant, which is doubled: יִכָּרֵת. In the imperative and the infinitive construct a prefixed he with an i-vowel stands before the doubled first consonant: הִשָּׁמֶר, לְהִלָּחֵם. The long vowel in the last syllable is typical of all these forms.

When the first root consonant is a guttural or resh, which cannot be doubled, the vowel before it is lengthened instead, and the doubling is not shown: יֵאָכֵל and יֵעָשֶׂה in Exodus 12:16. You will see this again with the weak roots.

sections.heading: How the Niphal relates to the Qal
body: Some Niphals are passive in relation to the Qal. The Qal verb 'bury' has the Niphal 'be buried': Rachel died and was buried (Genesis 35:19). Some are reflexive or middle: the Qal verb 'keep, guard' has the Niphal imperative in Deuteronomy 4:9, 'guard yourself', which stands next to a Qal imperative of the same verb. Some verbs are middle in a looser sense: where the Qal of 'see' says that someone saw something (Genesis 1:4), the Niphal says that someone was seen or appeared (Genesis 12:7).

Some Niphals are reciprocal, as the grammars describe them: the people involved act on each other, as when Amos asks whether two will walk together unless they have met by appointment (Amos 3:3). And some verbs occur in the Niphal as their ordinary form. The Niphal of שָׁבַע, 'swear', has no Qal with that sense, and the Niphal of לָחַם, 'fight', is the common form, while its Qal occurs only a few times and in poetry. Do not look for a passive sense here.

sections.heading: Reading the Niphal
body: First read the stem from the shape, then ask what the Niphal means for this root. If the Qal of the root is common, ask whether the Niphal is its passive ('is cut off'), its reflexive ('guards himself') or its middle ('appears'). If the Qal is rare or absent, treat the Niphal as the root's ordinary form and take its sense from the lexicon.
The person who does a Niphal passive is usually not named. When an agent is named, it is often introduced by a preposition, and the clause needs to be read as a whole.

misunderstandings: The Niphal is not simply 'the passive'. It is passive for some verbs, reflexive or middle for others, and for a few it is the only stem that the verb has.
The nun is not always visible. In the yiqtol, imperative and infinitives it has been absorbed into the following consonant, so look for the doubled first root consonant instead.
The doubled consonant of the Niphal yiqtol is not the doubled middle consonant of the Piel. In the Niphal it is the first root consonant, after the prefix.
The Niphal participle can look like the qatal. Check the vowel of the last syllable and the place of the word in the clause.

deeper.heading: The nun
body: Comparative grammar explains the nun of the Niphal as an old prefix with a reflexive or passive force that is also found in other Semitic languages, and the doubled consonant of the yiqtol as the nun assimilated to the letter that follows it. This is the standard explanation; it is not something that can be read from the Hebrew text itself.

examples.analysis: וַיֵּרָא is a Niphal wayyiqtol, third masculine singular, of the root that has the Qal 'see' in Genesis 1:4. The Niphal says that the LORD appeared. הַנִּרְאֶה is a Niphal participle with the article: 'the one who appeared'. Here the Niphal is middle: it is not 'was seen by someone' but 'showed himself'.

examples.analysis: הִשָּׁמֶר is a Niphal imperative, second masculine singular, with the prefix hi- and the first root consonant doubled. It is reflexive: 'guard yourself', 'take care'. The next verb, וּשְׁמֹר, is a Qal imperative of the same root, with the object 'your soul'. One root in two stems, side by side: the Qal acts on an object, the Niphal on the subject.
